lead: One transistor becomes three amplifiers depending on which terminal is signal ground. CE: voltage gain, output inverted. CB: gain without inversion, very low input resistance. CC (emitter follower): gain just under one, tiny output resistance. Bias and Q-point are unchanged; only the signal ports move. One device covers audio preamps, RF inputs and buffers.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.4 for the small-signal models, and Chapter 2.2 for the DC operating point these formulas sit on.

blocks.text: An amplifier has an input port, an output port and a common terminal. In a BJT the emitter, base and collector are the candidates. Ground one for signals — directly or through a capacitor that is a short at signal frequency — and the other two become input and output.

items: CE: emitter common; input at base, output at collector.
CB: base common; input at emitter, output at collector.
CC: collector common (AC ground through V_CC); input at base, output at emitter. This is the emitter follower.

blocks.text: The bias network is unchanged (Chapter 2.2), so the Q-point is the same. Coupling capacitors pass the signal and block DC; a bypass capacitor across R_E shorts it for signals, so R_E leaves the AC path.

blocks.where: r_e is the small-signal emitter resistance in ohms; V_T ≈ 26 mV is the thermal voltage at room temperature; I_E is the DC emitter current in A. At I_C ≈ I_E = 1 mA, r_e = 26 Ω.

blocks.text: Every derivation needs r_e, β and the resistors. Take r_o as infinite.
Signal enters the base through a coupling capacitor and leaves the collector. R1 and R2 set the base voltage, R_C is the collector resistor, and C_E bypasses R_E so the emitter is at AC ground.

items: With the emitter AC-grounded, looking into the base the transistor shows β r_e: base current i_b flows through r_e carrying i_e ≈ β i_b.
Collector current i_c = β i_b flows through R_C in parallel with the load R_L.
Output v_o = −i_c (R_C ∥ R_L); input v_i = i_b β r_e.
Divide: β cancels and the minus sign appears.

blocks.where: A_v is voltage gain (no units); R_C is the collector resistor and R_L the external load, both in ohms; r_e in ohms. The minus sign means 180° inversion: a rising input gives a falling collector.

blocks.text: R_in = R1 ∥ R2 ∥ β r_e ,  R_out ≈ R_C
blocks.where: R_in is resistance seen by the source at the base, R_out resistance seen looking back into the output with the source zeroed. Bias resistors appear in parallel with the transistor's own β r_e.

blocks.text: Without C_E, R_E stays in the signal path: A_v = −(R_C ∥ R_L)/(r_e + R_E) and R_in = R1 ∥ R2 ∥ β(r_e + R_E). Gain falls, input resistance rises, distortion falls — local feedback. CE has the highest voltage and current gain, so it is the usual first stage (Chapter 2.7).

sections.h3: Common base: no inversion, low input resistance

blocks.text: The base is held at AC ground by a bypass capacitor; the signal enters the emitter and leaves the collector through R_C.
Looking into the emitter you see r_e — about 26 Ω at 1 mA. Current gain is i_c/i_e = α = β/(β+1), below 1 (0.99 at β = 100). Voltage gain has the same size as CE but is positive.
A_v = +α (R_C ∥ R_L) / r_e ≈ (R_C ∥ R_L) / r_e ,  R_out ≈ R_C
blocks.where: A_v is positive, so there is no phase inversion. A rising emitter voltage lowers v_BE, so i_c falls, the drop across R_C falls, and the collector voltage rises.

blocks.text: CB is useful because its low input resistance matches a coaxial cable or antenna, and its input at the emitter avoids the Miller effect that limits CE at high frequency (Unit 3). It is also the upper transistor of a cascode (Chapter 2.8).
The collector is tied to V_CC, which is AC ground. Input at base, output at emitter across R_E ∥ R_L. The emitter follows the base, one v_BE below it.

blocks.where: A_v is just under 1 (0.987 at R_E = 2 kΩ, r_e = 26 Ω) and in phase with the input. The whole signal appears across the load except the small drop on r_e.

blocks.text: R_in = R1 ∥ R2 ∥ β (r_e + R_E ∥ R_L) ,  R_out ≈ r_e + (R1 ∥ R2 ∥ R_S) / β
blocks.where: R_S is the resistance of the source driving the base. A resistance at the emitter is multiplied by β when seen from the base; a resistance at the base is divided by β when seen from the emitter.

blocks.text: At I_C = 1 mA (r_e = 26 Ω), R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ and R_S = 1 kΩ: R1 ∥ R2 = 8.25 kΩ; with R_S in parallel, 892 Ω; divided by β = 100 gives 8.9 Ω; R_out ≈ 26 + 8.9 = 34.9 Ω. CE would be about 3 kΩ.

That is why the follower is a buffer: high R_in, low R_out, no voltage loss. It drives cables, small loudspeakers through a power stage, or a low-resistance next block. It has current gain, so it amplifies power. It appears inside op-amps (Unit 5) and class AB drivers (Unit 3).

figure.caption: The common-emitter stage inverts and gives voltage gain; the emitter follower gives no voltage gain but the lowest output resistance of the three.

spec.title: One transistor, three connections
spec.aria: A four-row table of voltage gain, current gain, input resistance, output resistance and phase for the common-emitter, common-base and common-collector connections.

examples.question: A CE amplifier uses a BJT with I_C = 1 mA, β = 100, R_C = 3 kΩ, R_L = 6 kΩ, R1 = 47 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ. Take V_T = 26 mV and ignore r_o. Find (a) r_e, (b) A_v and phase shift, (c) R_in, (d) R_out. (e) The same transistor is reconnected as an emitter follower with R_E = 2 kΩ, no external load, driven from R_S = 1 kΩ; find A_v and R_out.
steps: R_C ∥ R_L = (3 kΩ × 6 kΩ)/(3 kΩ + 6 kΩ) = 2 kΩ.
examples.answer: r_e = 26 Ω, A_v = −76.92 with 180° phase shift, R_in = 1.98 kΩ, R_out = 3 kΩ; as an emitter follower A_v = 0.9872 and R_out = 34.92 Ω.
examples.check:
VT = 26e-3
IC = 1e-3
beta = 100
RC = 3e3
RL = 6e3
R1 = 47e3
R2 = 10e3
RE = 2e3
RS = 1e3
re = VT/IC
print(round(re, 2))
rp = RC*RL/(RC+RL)
Av = -rp/re
print(round(Av, 2))
brp = beta*re
r12 = R1*R2/(R1+R2)
Rin = r12*brp/(r12+brp)
print(round(Rin, 1))
print(round(RC, 1))
Avcc = RE/(re+RE)
print(round(Avcc, 4))
rpar = 1/(1/r12 + 1/RS)
Routcc = re + rpar/beta
print(round(Routcc, 2))

traps: Writing R_out of the follower as high because it has a collector resistor. It is the lowest of the three, tens of ohms.
Forgetting CE inversion when cascading. Two CE stages give 360°, back in phase.
Using r_e = 26 mV/I_B. At β = 100 that is 100 times too large.
Thinking gain below one means no amplification. The follower has current gain, so power gain.
Ignoring R_L. Gain formulas use R_C ∥ R_L; a load drops gain at once.

quiz.q: What is r_e for a BJT carrying I_C = 1 mA at room temperature?
In the CB connection, which terminal is common, and what is the phase shift?
quiz.a: The base is common (AC ground); phase shift is 0°, no inversion.

quiz.q: Why does CE invert while CB does not?
quiz.a: CE: rising base voltage raises i_c; the drop i_c R_C rises, so collector voltage falls. CB: rising emitter voltage lowers v_BE, so i_c falls; the drop across R_C falls, so collector voltage rises.

quiz.q: A CB stage has I_C = 2 mA, α = 0.98, R_C = 4.7 kΩ and no load. Find r_e, A_v and R_in.
A CE stage has I_C = 0.5 mA, β = 150, R_C = 10 kΩ, no load, and unbypassed R_E = 200 Ω. Find r_e, A_v and resistance looking into the base.
quiz.a: r_e = 26 mV / 0.5 mA = 52 Ω. A_v = −R_C/(r_e + R_E) = −10000/252 = −39.68. Base input resistance = β(r_e + R_E) = 150 × 252 = 37.8 kΩ.

quiz.q: Explain why the emitter follower has input resistance in kilohms and output resistance in tens of ohms.
quiz.a: Any change in emitter voltage changes v_BE, so the transistor adjusts current to oppose it — the emitter follows the base. This feedback multiplies an emitter resistance by β when seen from the base, and divides a base resistance by β when seen from the emitter.

quiz.q: A CE stage has its emitter bypass capacitor removed. State what happens to A_v, R_in and distortion, with reasons.
quiz.a: A_v falls from −(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e to −(R_C ∥ R_L)/(r_e + R_E), because R_E now carries signal current. R_in rises from R1 ∥ R2 ∥ β r_e to R1 ∥ R2 ∥ β(r_e + R_E). Distortion falls because R_E introduces local negative feedback.

beyond: Not for the exam. Inside ICs the emitter follower is the buffer that drives a capacitive load without eating bandwidth; op-amp output stages use it (Unit 5). Radio front ends use common-base and cascode input stages because the emitter meets a 50 Ω antenna naturally. Audio power amplifiers use the follower as the driver for a class AB pair (Unit 3).
